dutch: Waar kan ik de melk vinden?
english: Where can I find the milk?
scenario: You are in the supermarket and cannot see the milk. Ask a worker where it is.
grammar: Question word + modal + subject; the infinitive vinden comes last.
variation: Waar kan ik het brood vinden?

dutch: Ik wil graag twee broodjes, alstublieft.
english: I would like two rolls, please.
scenario: You are at the bakery counter. Politely order two bread rolls.
grammar: Ik wil graag + noun is a useful polite request.
variation: Ik wil graag een koffie, alstublieft.

dutch: Kan ik met de kaart betalen?
english: Can I pay by card?
scenario: You are at the till with your bank card. Ask if you can pay with it.
grammar: In a yes/no question, kan comes before ik; betalen comes last.

english: How much does this bag cost?
scenario: You like a bag but see no price tag. Ask how much it costs.
grammar: Tas is a de-word, so use deze for this bag.

dutch: Heeft u ook een kleinere maat?
english: Do you also have a smaller size?
scenario: The shirt is too big. Ask the shop assistant if they have a smaller size.
grammar: U is polite you; kleiner takes -e before the de-word maat.
variation: Heeft u ook een grotere maat?

english: I do not need a bag.
scenario: The cashier asks about a bag. Say you do not need one.
grammar: Geen negates an indefinite noun: geen zak.

english: May I have the receipt, please?
scenario: You have just paid. Politely ask for the receipt.
grammar: Mag ik + noun is a common shortened request.

english: These apples are cheaper.
scenario: You are comparing prices. Point out that these apples are cheaper.
grammar: Plural nouns use deze; zijn agrees with plural appels.

dutch: Ik zoek een cadeau voor mijn vriendin.
english: I am looking for a gift for my girlfriend.
scenario: You are looking around a shop. Tell the assistant you are searching for a gift for your girlfriend.
grammar: Mijn means my and stays the same with de- and het-nouns.
variation: Ik zoek een cadeau voor mijn moeder.

english: I will take this one, thank you.
scenario: You have chosen one item. Tell the seller you will take this one and thank them.
grammar: Deze can stand alone for a de-noun or plural items.

dutch: Kunt u dat nog eens uitleggen?
english: Can you explain that again?
cue: Ask the teacher to explain again.
scenario: You did not understand the teacher. Politely ask them to explain it again.
grammar: Kunt u is polite; uitleggen is the infinitive at the end.

english: I do not understand this question.
scenario: You are looking at an exercise. Say that you do not understand this question.
grammar: Vraag is a de-word: deze vraag. Niet negates begrijpen here.

english: What does this word mean?
scenario: You see a word you do not know. Ask what it means.
grammar: Woord is a het-word, so use dit woord.

english: May I ask something quickly?
scenario: You want to interrupt the teacher briefly. Ask if you may ask something.
grammar: Mag + ik + infinitive at the end; even softens the request.

dutch: Ik heb mijn huiswerk al gemaakt.
english: I have already done my homework.
scenario: The teacher asks about homework. Say you have already done it.
grammar: Perfect tense: heb + past participle gemaakt. Mijn means my.
variation: Ik heb mijn opdracht al gemaakt.

english: When do we have to hand this in?
scenario: You need to know the deadline. Ask when you have to hand this in.
grammar: Modal moeten + infinitive inleveren; it stays together here.

english: My pen is on the table.
scenario: Someone asks where your pen is. Say it is lying on the table.
grammar: Dutch often uses ligt for an object lying somewhere.

english: Tomorrow I am going to school.
scenario: A classmate asks about your plans. Say you are going to school tomorrow.
grammar: Morgen comes first; ga remains second, before ik.

dutch: Ik ben te laat omdat mijn trein vertraging heeft.
english: I am late because my train is delayed.
scenario: You arrive late to class. Explain that it is because your train is delayed.
grammar: After omdat, the conjugated verb heeft goes to the end.
variation: Ik ben te laat omdat mijn bus vertraging heeft.

english: Can we practise together?
scenario: You want a study partner. Suggest practising together.
grammar: We uses the plural verb kunnen; oefenen comes last.

dutch: Van welk spoor vertrekt de trein?
english: From which platform does the train depart?
scenario: You are at the station. Ask which platform the train leaves from.
grammar: Van welk spoor asks from which railway track or platform.
variation: Van welk spoor vertrekt de trein naar Gent?

english: Do I need to change trains here?
scenario: You are not sure about your route. Ask if you have to change trains here.
grammar: Moet starts the question; overstappen is the infinitive at the end.

english: Does this train go to Bruges?
scenario: You are about to board. Ask if this train goes to Bruges.
grammar: Trein is a de-word: deze trein. Gaat starts the yes/no question.

dutch: Ik wil een ticket naar Gent, alstublieft.
english: I would like a ticket to Ghent, please.
scenario: You are at the ticket desk. Ask politely for a ticket to Ghent.
grammar: Naar marks the destination: naar Gent.
variation: Ik wil een ticket naar Brussel, alstublieft.

dutch: Hoe laat komt de trein aan?
english: What time does the train arrive?
scenario: You are waiting for a friend. Ask what time the train arrives.
grammar: Aankomen separates in the main clause: komt ... aan.
variation: Hoe laat komt de bus aan?

english: Is this seat free?
scenario: You see an empty seat. Ask if the seat is free.
grammar: Plaats is a de-word; vrij has no -e after is.

dutch: Mijn trein heeft tien minuten vertraging.
english: My train is ten minutes delayed.
scenario: You are texting a friend. Tell them your train is ten minutes late.
grammar: Heeft vertraging means is delayed; duration comes before vertraging.
variation: Mijn trein heeft vijf minuten vertraging.

dutch: Waar kan ik mijn ticket kopen?
english: Where can I buy my ticket?
cue: Find the ticket machine or office.
scenario: You need a ticket and see no machine. Ask where you can buy one.
grammar: Kan comes before ik in the question; kopen comes last.
variation: Waar kan ik een ticket kopen?

dutch: Ik stap bij de volgende halte uit.
english: I am getting off at the next stop.
cue: Say where you are getting off.
scenario: You are on the bus. Tell someone you are getting off at the next stop.
grammar: Uitstappen separates: ik stap ... uit.

dutch: Kunt u mij helpen met mijn bagage?
english: Can you help me with my luggage?
scenario: Your suitcase is heavy. Politely ask someone to help with your luggage.
grammar: Mij is the object me; mijn is possessive my.
variation: Kunt u mij helpen met mijn ticket?

english: Where are my keys?
scenario: You are about to leave and cannot find your keys. Ask where they are.
grammar: Plural sleutels uses zijn; mijn stays unchanged.

english: I am cooking.
cue: Say what you are doing now.
scenario: Someone calls and asks what you are doing. Say you are cooking.
grammar: Zijn + aan het + infinitive describes an ongoing activity.

dutch: Heb je de deur op slot gedaan?
english: Have you locked the door?
scenario: You wonder if a friend locked up. Ask if they locked the door.
grammar: Perfect question: heb + je + past participle gedaan.

dutch: Ik heb de afwas al gedaan.
english: I have already washed the dishes.
scenario: Your housemate asks about chores. Say you have already done the dishes.
grammar: Heb + gedaan is the perfect tense; al means already.
variation: Ik heb de was al gedaan.

english: Can you open the window?
cue: Ask someone to open the window.
scenario: The room is stuffy. Ask someone if they can open the window.
grammar: With je after the verb, use kun; openmaken stays together after the modal.

english: This is your cup.
scenario: You hand someone a cup. Tell them it is their cup.
grammar: Dit refers to the het-word kopje; jouw means your.

dutch: Na het werk fiets ik naar huis.
english: After work I cycle home.
scenario: Someone asks about your evening routine. Say that after work you cycle home.
grammar: Na het werk takes first position; fiets comes second, before ik.
variation: Na school fiets ik naar huis.

dutch: Er staat melk in de koelkast.
english: There is milk in the fridge.
scenario: A friend wants a drink. Tell them there is milk in the fridge.
grammar: Er introduces something present; staat describes its position here.
variation: Er staat water in de koelkast.

english: I am tidying my room.
scenario: Your parents come over. Say you are tidying your room.
grammar: Opruimen separates in the main clause: ruim ... op.

english: Shall we eat together?
scenario: It is dinner time. Suggest eating together.
grammar: Zullen we + infinitive is a common suggestion.

english: I speak a little Dutch.
scenario: You meet someone new. Tell them you speak a little Dutch.
grammar: Een beetje means a little; spreek agrees with ik.

english: Can you speak a little more slowly?
scenario: Someone speaks too fast. Ask them to speak a bit more slowly.
grammar: Langzamer is the comparative of langzaam; spreken comes last.

english: How are you?
scenario: You meet a friend. Ask how they are doing.
grammar: Hoe gaat het met ... is a fixed expression.

english: I live in Roeselare.
scenario: Someone asks where you live. Say you live in Roeselare.
grammar: In marks the city where you live.

english: Where are you from?
scenario: You meet someone at a party. Ask where they are from.
grammar: Waar ... vandaan asks about origin; kom loses -t before je.

english: Do you have time tomorrow?
scenario: You want to make plans. Ask if they have time tomorrow.
grammar: Heb loses -t when je follows it in the question.

english: I cannot come today.
scenario: You must cancel. Tell them you cannot come today.
grammar: Kan + infinitive komen; niet negates the action.

dutch: Zullen we om drie uur afspreken?
english: Shall we meet at three o’clock?
scenario: You are arranging a meeting. Suggest meeting at three o’clock.
grammar: Om introduces a clock time; afspreken stays together after zullen.
variation: Zullen we om vier uur afspreken?

dutch: Ik ben moe, maar ik voel me goed.
english: I am tired, but I feel good.
scenario: A friend asks how you are. Say you are tired, but you feel good.
grammar: Maar keeps main-clause order; zich voelen uses me with ik.
variation: Ik ben druk, maar ik voel me goed.

english: Thank you for your help.
scenario: Someone has helped you. Thank them for their help.
grammar: Voor follows bedankt; je can mean your before a noun.
